newsitem.title: TURKEY: U.S. says in touch with EU over wheat subsidies.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says in touch with EU over wheat subsidies.

text.p: The United States has been in informal contact with the European Union to try to persuade it not to use wheat export subsidies on the world grain market, a U.S. government official said on Tuesday.

But Washington has not decided whether to restore its own aid in response to last week's EU decision to grant commercial subsidies for the first time in over a year, Craig Thorn, division director for trade policy with Europe, Africa, Middle East and Asia at the U.S. Department of Agriculture said.

"We have been in contact with Brussels informally to try to convince them that this is not a road we want to go down. But the United States has not made a decision (on its own actions)," Thorn told the Second Annual World Grain and Feed Conference in southern Turkey.
The U.S. government has promised to "fight fire with fire" if necessary to counter EU wheat subsidies.

After a pause of 16 months, these are now being used to close a gap between European prices and lower ones on the world market where wheat is again in good supply after record low stocks and soaring prices earlier this year.

Subsidies by the United States and Europe led to a bitter trade confrontation in the 1980s and early part of this decade, but were withdrawn in May 1995 as world prices began rising. They reached a record in April this year before sliding again.
Thorn said he did not think either the current wheat or barley markets justified a return to subsidies and noted concern about a return to penalising subsidised competition.

Both sides are now limited by the Uruguay Round world trade pact, setting declining quotas on export subsidies from mid-1995 until the turn of the century. But analysts say there is plenty of scope for a subsidy spat within the trade ceilings this year.
Much will depend on whether either side believes the other is being too aggressive and driving the world price of grain lower, delegates at the conference said.
In this area, the United States is on a back foot this year as its exports are expected to slip after a difficult harvest. In Europe and several other regions crops have jumped sharply.

Officials monitoring the issue said the EU appeared to have informally defended to Washington its decision to use subsidies of eight dollars a tonne to sell wheat, but there had been no formal diplomatic exchange with the United States.
